title: Heidi
author: Johanna Spyri
short_summary: Orphaned young Heidi is left with her gruff grandfather high in the Swiss Alps, and quickly comes to love the mountain, the goats and her friend Peter the goatherd. Then she is taken away to Frankfurt as a companion for Clara, a rich girl who cannot walk — and although she is kind to Clara and learns to read there, the longing for the mountain makes her ill in a way nobody understands until the doctor does.
extended_summary:
Heidi is brought up the mountain by her Aunt Dete and left with the grandfather everyone in the village calls the Alm-Uncle, a man who has not come down to church in years. Heidi is not frightened of him. She sleeps in the hayloft on a bed of hay, with a round window she can look out of at the mountains, and spends her days on the high pasture with Peter the goatherd and the two goats, Little Swan and Little Bear. Down in the village she becomes the favourite of Peter's blind grandmother, who cannot chew the hard black bread she is given.

Dete comes back and takes Heidi to Frankfurt to be a companion to Clara Sesemann, who uses a wheelchair. There Heidi is taught manners by Fräulein Rottenmeier, learns to read at last when Clara's grandmother gives her a picture book, and quietly saves up every soft white roll from the table to carry home to the blind grandmother. She says nothing about being unhappy, and instead begins walking in her sleep: the household thinks the house is haunted until the doctor watches one night, finds Heidi at the front door and diagnoses homesickness so severe that she must be sent home at once.

Home on the mountain, Heidi recovers, and the grandfather comes back down to the village and to the church. Clara visits the following summer. When Peter, jealous of her, sends the empty wheelchair rolling down the mountainside, Clara is left with no choice but to try to stand — and with the goats' milk, the air and Heidi holding one arm, she learns to walk.

questions.prompt: Where does Heidi sleep on her very first night at her grandfather's hut?

options: In the hayloft, beside a round window
In her grandfather's own bed by the stove
On a bench beside the fire downstairs
In the goat shed, wrapped in a blanket

questions.explanation: She makes her own bed out of hay and is delighted with it, because the round window in the wall looks straight out at the mountains. That window matters later: in Frankfurt she cannot see out of any of the windows, and it is one of the things that quietly breaks her heart.

questions.prompt: In Frankfurt, Heidi hides a soft white roll from the table every single day. Why?

options: For Peter's grandmother, who cannot chew hard bread
Because she is afraid of being hungry later on
To feed the goats when she finally gets home
To give to the poor children she sees in the street

questions.explanation: The blind grandmother's bread is hard and black and she has almost no teeth left. Heidi says nothing to anyone and simply collects rolls in her cupboard week after week — a child's plan, faithfully carried out, and it is the first thing she thinks about when she is finally allowed home.

questions.prompt: The doctor watches one night, finds Heidi at the front door in her nightgown, and gives the family his diagnosis: the child is ill with ___.
questions.explanation: He says it plainly, and insists she be sent home immediately. Spyri treats homesickness as a real illness with physical symptoms, which is unusual and quite modern: nobody in the house has thought to ask Heidi how she feels, and she has been too well-mannered to say.

questions.prompt: For several nights the Sesemann household is convinced the house is haunted. What is really happening?

options: Heidi is walking in her sleep and opening the door
Sebastian has been letting a stray cat inside
The wind is blowing the shutters open each night
Clara has been wheeling herself about in the dark

questions.explanation: Heidi gets up asleep, goes downstairs and unbolts the front door — she is trying to go home. The 'ghost' terrifies the servants for days, and it is the doctor, not the family, who works out that the ghost is a desperately unhappy child.

questions.prompt: Put the events of Heidi's story in the order they happen.

items: Aunt Dete leaves Heidi with her grandfather on the Alm
Heidi makes herself a bed of hay in the loft
Dete takes Heidi away to Frankfurt to be Clara's companion
Clara's grandmother teaches Heidi to read at last
The doctor discovers who the ghost in the house is
Clara takes her first steps on the mountain

questions.explanation: The book is built as a there-and-back-again with a second visit at the end: Heidi is carried down to the city, sent back up, and then the city comes to her. Notice that Clara only gets better on the mountain — the book is quite insistent about where health comes from.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their part in Heidi's story.

right: The goatherd who takes the goats up the mountain
The blind woman who waits for the white rolls
The housekeeper who decides what a young lady may do
The girl in the wheelchair who asks Heidi to stay

questions.explanation: Two of these people need Heidi and two of them manage her. It is not a coincidence that the two who need her are poor and the two who manage her are not — Spyri is very clear about where Heidi is treated as a person.

questions.prompt: Sort each detail by where it belongs in Heidi's life.

options.label: A bed of hay under a round window
Goat's milk and toasted cheese for supper
Two goats called Little Swan and Little Bear
Rules about how a young lady sits at table
A cupboard slowly filling with white rolls
Windows that show nothing but a stone wall

questions.explanation: Everything in the right-hand column is more expensive than anything in the left, and Heidi is miserable in it. Spyri does not make the Sesemanns cruel — they are kind and generous — which is exactly what makes the point: kindness is not the same as understanding what a person needs.

questions.prompt: When Clara comes to stay on the mountain, Peter sends her empty wheelchair rolling down the mountainside. Why does he do it?

options: He is jealous: Clara has taken Heidi's attention
He believes the chair is stopping Clara walking
He wants to make Clara stay on the mountain longer
He is paid by someone in the village to do it

questions.explanation: Peter has lost his friend to a newcomer and cannot say so, so he destroys the newcomer's chair instead. The book does not excuse him — he is sick with guilt for days — but it does let the worst thing he ever does turn out to be the thing that gets Clara on her feet.

questions.prompt: Aunt Dete takes Heidi away from the mountain to Frankfurt without telling her the truth about where they are going or that she will not be coming straight back. Dete believes she is giving Heidi a much better future. Was she right to do it? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both sides can earn full marks. A strong 'she was wrong' answer notices the lie, the illness that followed, and that nobody asked Heidi. A strong 'she had a point' answer notices that Heidi learns to read in Frankfurt, meets Clara and the grandmother, and that a child living with an old hermit on a mountain really had no schooling at all. Accept either, argued from the book.

questions.prompt: Heidi spent months quietly saving white rolls for a blind old woman she could not even write to. Think of one person you know. If you were far away for a long time, what small thing would you save or bring back for them, and why that thing in particular?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer names one specific small object — not money, not 'a present' — and explains why it suits that particular person, which is what makes Heidi's rolls so moving: they are useless to anyone except one woman with no teeth.

questions.prompt: Heidi's grandfather keeps two goats, and Heidi learns their names at once: Little Swan and Little ___.
questions.explanation: The white one and the brown one, and Heidi can tell every goat in Peter's herd apart within days. Learning the animals' names is how she takes possession of the mountain — and the names are the first thing she talks about in Frankfurt.

questions.prompt: What happens to Clara during her summer on the mountain?

options: She learns to walk, a few steps at a time
She decides to stay and live with the grandfather
She becomes too ill and has to be taken home
She teaches Heidi and Peter to read properly

questions.explanation: Goat's milk, mountain air, and being made to try because her chair is at the bottom of a ravine. Spyri is writing a slightly magical version of medicine here, but the important part is the order of events: Clara only tries once there is no alternative left.
